Posterior predictive checks confirm adequate model fit (predicted response rate $0.593$ vs.\ observed $0.599$; Appendix~\ref{app:ppc}). The global shrinkage scale $\hat{\sigma}_c = 2.40$ confirms substantial inter-model heterogeneity ($\bar{c} = 2.50$, aligning with the strong-contamination regime in synthetic validation). Notably, sequential estimation yields near-zero contamination estimates ($\bar{c} \approx 0$), demonstrating that without joint modeling, contamination effects are entirely absorbed into ability estimates $\hat{\theta}$---precisely the omitted variable bias predicted by the theoretical analysis (Section~\ref{sec:confounding}). -Ranking improvement ($\Delta\tau = +0.071$) is not statistically significant at $N = 8$ (bootstrap 95\% CI crosses zero). +Ranking improvement ($\Delta\tau = +0.071$) is not statistically significant at $N = 8$ (bootstrap 95\% CI crosses zero). Post-hoc power analysis indicates $N \approx 17$ is needed for 80\% power to detect this effect size (Appendix~\ref{app:power}). Synthetic replication at matched scale ($N = 8$, $I = 176$, $J = 9$) confirms a significant effect across 20 seeds (Wilcoxon $p < 0.002$; Appendix~\ref{app:synthetic_calibration}).

The MCMC sampler achieves rank-normalized split-$\hat{R} \leq 1.03$ across all parameters with zero divergent transitions and minimum bulk ESS of 174 (217 for model-level parameters $\theta_n$, $c_n$, $d_j$). These values satisfy the traditional convergence thresholds ($\hat{R} < 1.05$, ESS $> 100$; \citealp{gelman2013bda}) but do not meet the stricter criteria of \citet{vehtari2021rhat} ($\hat{R} < 1.01$, ESS $> 400$), which may contribute to posterior overconfidence (synthetic CI coverage 71\%; see Limitations); we report point estimates and rank orderings as primary results. Model and judge facets show acceptable fit (all infit/outfit MNSQ within $[0.63, 1.07]$; item-level diagnostics in Appendix). Posterior predictive checks confirm adequate model fit (predicted response rate $0.593$ vs.\ observed $0.599$; Appendix~\ref{app:ppc}). Contamination susceptibility $\hat{c}_n$ exhibits a gradient by model age, directionally consistent with known training data exposure. Estimated $\hat{c}_n$ exceeds 1.0 for the four oldest models: GPT-3.5-Turbo ($\hat{c}_n = 5.60$), GPT-4-0613 ($4.20$), Qwen2.5-72B ($3.00$), and LLaMA-3.3-70B ($2.50$). The most recent models show low estimated contamination: GPT-4o ($0.88$) and GPT-4o-mini ($0.93$). The global shrinkage scale $\hat{\sigma}_c = 2.40$ confirms substantial inter-model heterogeneity ($\bar{c} = 2.50$, aligning with the strong-contamination regime in synthetic validation). Notably, sequential estimation yields near-zero contamination estimates ($\bar{c} \approx 0$), demonstrating that without joint modeling, contamination effects are entirely absorbed into ability estimates $\hat{\theta}$---precisely the omitted variable bias predicted by the theoretical analysis (Section~\ref{sec:confounding}). A per-model diagnostic (Table~\ref{tab:bias_absorption}) reveals that MFRM-only inflates ability estimates for the most contaminated models by up to 0.79 logits (GPT-3.5-Turbo), while deflating estimates for the least contaminated models by up to 0.40 logits (GPT-4o). Judge severity $d_j$ separates by provenance: proprietary judges tend to score more strictly (e.g., Claude Opus $+0.60$, GPT-5.5 $+0.53$) than open-source judges (e.g., Mistral $-0.74$, LLaMA $-0.42$); full $d_j$ values for all nine judges are reported in Table~\ref{tab:judge_severity}. We identify six limitations. First, although Theorem~\ref{thm:sufficient} requires only a connected design, the current evaluation achieves 44.7\% fill rate (5{,}661 of 12{,}672 potential cells); sparser designs may compromise identifiability of $c_n$ for models with few observed exposed items. Relatedly, sparse observations per item produce elevated item-level mean-square residuals (92/176 items), though model- and judge-level fit remains acceptable. Second, Stage~2 exposure estimation relies on a reference model anchor (gpt-4-0314), and exposure estimate quality depends on the anchor remaining uncontaminated relative to the benchmark; as benchmarks age, anchor validity should be periodically re-assessed. Third, the current evaluation uses a single benchmark (Arena-Hard) with eight target models; post-hoc power analysis indicates that detecting $\Delta\tau = 0.071$ at $\alpha = 0.05$ requires $N \approx 17$ models for 80\% power, while $N = 8$ yields approximately 50\% power, explaining the non-significant bootstrap result. Generalization to other benchmarks and larger model populations remains to be verified. Fourth, empirical CI coverage differs by parameter type: ability estimates $\theta$ approach nominal coverage at moderate sample sizes (${\sim}$90\% at $N = 8$), while contamination susceptibility $c_n$ exhibits moderate posterior overconfidence (71\% at $N = 50$, 58\% at $N = 8$; \citealp{talts2018sbc}). The $c_n$ under-coverage reflects the multiplicative coupling $c_n \cdot e_i$ and the HalfNormal prior's boundary constraint at $c_n = 0$, which systematically narrows posterior credible intervals. Point estimates and rank orderings ($\tau = 0.857$) are unaffected; $c_n$ estimates are best interpreted as directional diagnostics rather than calibrated intervals. Fifth, while self-evaluation sensitivity analysis (Appendix~\ref{app:self_eval}) confirms robust rankings when excluding self-judging observations, a more comprehensive analysis removing overlapping models entirely from the judge panel has not been conducted. Sixth, the bilinear contamination term $c_n \cdot e_i$ assumes rank-1 structure---a single latent dimension of contamination susceptibility per model. In practice, contamination may be domain-specific (e.g., coding vs.\ reasoning items), requiring a higher-rank decomposition $\sum_r c_{nr} \cdot e_{ir}$ that the current model does not capture.
